context: systems-integration led · signalling/CBTC & the trial-running safety-case own the back end; deep civil (tunnels, viaducts, station boxes) is the enabling backbone

brief.intro: A rail or metro transit system is not one building but a whole corridor — track, structures (tunnels, viaducts, at-grade formation) and stations — tied together by railway systems: traction power, signalling, telecoms and control. Unlike a building project, the civil works (tunnels, viaducts, trackbed) are the enabling backbone rather than the schedule driver once they are handed over section by section; what actually governs completion is the systems package and the safety-case process that must prove the whole line before a single passenger rides it. Traction power, energised in stages section by section, and signalling/train-control — interlocking, train detection, and on driverless lines CBTC — are first-class disciplines, not secondary MEP, because a line simply cannot run without them. Commissioning therefore runs as a long chain — system installation → subsystem testing → system integration testing → trial running and dynamic testing → the independent safety-case sign-off — and this back end typically consumes a large share of total programme duration. Civil works are usually handed over in sections to let systems installation start early on completed lengths, so the interface between civil completion and systems mobilisation, section by section, is itself a key planning discipline.

scope.name: Enabling & site works
scope.desc: Compounds, access, utility diversions and early works ahead of the civil main works.

scope.name: Civil structures
scope.desc: Trackbed formation, tunnels (bored/cut-and-cover), viaducts, station boxes and cross-passages.

scope.name: Trackform
scope.desc: Ballasted or slab track, rail welding and alignment.

scope.name: Traction power
scope.desc: Substations, OHLE/third-rail, cabling and sectioning to energise the line in stages.

scope.name: Signalling & train control
scope.desc: Interlocking, train detection, and on automated lines CBTC — the system that actually lets trains run safely.

scope.name: Telecoms & SCADA
scope.desc: Radio/GSM-R, PA/PIS, and the SCADA/control-centre system that ties the whole line together.

scope.name: Stations & platforms
scope.desc: Platform structures, escalators/lifts, fare gates and public-area fit-out (station-box detail sits in a companion metro-station playbook).

scope.name: Tunnel ventilation & life safety
scope.desc: Jet fans/ventilation shafts, fire/smoke detection, cause-and-effect systems for tunnel and station sections.

scope.name: Earthing & bonding
scope.desc: Traction return, stray-current protection and structure bonding along the whole alignment.

scope.name: Testing & commissioning
scope.desc: System-by-system testing, integration testing, trial running, dynamic testing and safety-case sign-off before passenger service.

glossary.plain: the overhead wire or track-level rail that supplies traction power to trains.
Communications-Based Train Control — a signalling system that lets trains run closer together, sometimes driverless.
the safety logic that stops conflicting train movements, e.g. two trains being routed onto the same track.
running trains on the completed line, without passengers, to prove reliability before service starts.
the formal evidence package that proves the whole system is safe enough for a regulator to approve passenger service.
traction current that leaks into the ground and can corrode buried metal structures if not controlled by bonding/earthing.
energising traction power in defined sections so testing and construction can proceed safely on the de-energised sections.
the software and control room that monitors and operates power, signalling and station systems for the whole line.

must_get_right: Hand over civil sections progressively so systems installation can start early — waiting for 100% civil completion before systems mobilise is the single biggest cause of overrun.
Treat signalling/CBTC integration and the safety-case process as the true critical path, not the civil works — protect real time for it, not a punch-list allowance.
Sequence traction-power sectioning carefully — testing and construction crews need de-energised sections, so energisation staging must be planned, not improvised.
Plan trial running and dynamic testing as a distinct, lengthy phase with its own float — re-tests and regulator observation runs are normal, not exceptional.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress, usually broken into civil, systems and stations sub-networks that roll up to one master schedule. Activities carry durations in working days; the network is calculated (F9) with no artificial constraints beyond contractual milestones. Total float is kept ≥ 0 in the baseline.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Civil works (tunnelling, viaduct, station box) typically run continuous shift patterns driven by the construction method (TBM advance, jump-form cycle); systems installation runs possession-based access once track is handed over; testing and trial running run an extended calendar to make best use of scarce possession windows.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: The driving path runs civil handover (sectional) → trackform → traction-power sectioning & energisation → signalling/CBTC installation and data build → telecoms/SCADA integration → system integration testing → trial running & dynamic testing → safety-case sign-off. Once civil sections are handed over, signalling/CBTC integration and the trial-running/safety-case regime — not the remaining civil works — become the true driver of the completion date.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: Civil sections are handed over progressively to a pre-agreed interface schedule; the systems supplier's design is frozen ahead of equipment procurement; possession windows for testing are secured with the infrastructure/track authority; a single systems-integration contractor coordinates all disciplines. Any change to these invalidates the baseline dates.

sections.heading: Procurement & long-lead items
sections.body: The schedule is systems-led at the back end. The following are tracked as milestones and drive the network:

rows: Signalling / CBTC system (design, factory build & FAT)

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Systems installation depends on possession windows on a live or partially-live corridor, which are limited and shared across trades; dynamic testing at line speed needs exclusive possession and is scheduled around traffic/operations constraints. Signalling and CBTC engineers are a specialised, scarce resource contested across the whole programme.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Principal risks: civil-to-systems handover slippage, signalling/CBTC software and data-build delays, and safety-case observations that trigger re-testing. Schedule contingency is concentrated before system integration testing and before the safety-case submission rather than spread thinly across activities.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (summary) to the client/authority; controlled at Level 3; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead for site and testing teams — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
